'''''Populus nigra''''', the '''black poplar''', is a [[species]] of [[Populus sect. Aigeiros|cottonwood]] poplar, the [[type species]] of section ''Aigeiros'' of the genus ''[[Populus]]'', native to Europe, southwest and central Asia, and northwest Africa.<ref name=fe>Flora Europaea: [http://rbg-web2.rbge.org.uk/cgi-bin/nph-readbtree.pl/feout?FAMILY_XREF=&GENUS_XREF=Populus+&SPECIES_XREF=nigra&TAXON_NAME_XREF=&RANK= ''Populus nigra'']</ref>

==Description==
Black poplars are medium- to large-sized [[deciduous]] [[tree]]s, reaching 20–30 m, and rarely 40 m tall. Their [[leaf|leaves]] are diamond-shaped to triangular, 5–8 cm long and 6–8 cm broad, and green on both surfaces.<ref name=rushforth>Rushforth, K. (1999). ''Trees of Britain and Europe''. Collins. {{ISBN|0-00-220013-9}}.</ref> Normally, their trunks achieve up to 1.5 m in diameter, but some unusual individual trees in France have grown old enough to have much larger trunks – more than 3 metres DBH ([[Diameter at breast height|Diameter at Breast Height]]).

The species is [[Wiktionary:dioecious|dioecious]] (male and female flowers are on different plants), with flowers in [[catkin]]s and [[pollination]] achieved by the wind.  The black poplar grows in low-lying areas of moist ground.<ref name="Woodland Trust">{{cite web|title=Black Poplar|url=https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/learn/british-trees/native-trees/black-poplar/|website=The Woodland Trust|access-date=July 12, 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714214410/https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/learn/british-trees/native-trees/black-poplar/|archive-date=July 14, 2014}}</ref>  Like most other [[pioneer species]], the tree is characterized by rapid growth and is  able to colonize open areas quickly.<ref name="broeck03"/> 
[[File:Poplar seed tufts 2009 G1.jpg|thumb|upright|right|Poplar seed tufts]]

===Subspecies===
Three [[subspecies]] are ''established'' and some botanists distinguish a fourth:<ref name=fe/><ref name=rushforth/>
*''P. n.'' subsp. ''nigra''. Central and eastern Europe. Leaves and shoots glabrous (hairless); bark grey-brown, thick and furrowed.
[[Image:Burr on Black poplar.JPG|right|thumb|Burrs and normal bark on a black poplar tree (subspecies ''betulifolia'') in Ayrshire, Scotland.]]
*''P. n.''  subsp. ''betulifolia'' (Pursh) W.Wettst. North-west Europe ([[France]], [[Great Britain]], [[Ireland]]). Leaf veins and shoots finely downy; bark grey-brown, thick and furrowed, often with heavy [[Burl|burr]]s, trunk usually heavily leaning.
*''P. n.''  subsp. ''caudina'' (Ten.) Bugała. Mediterranean region, also southwest Asia if var. ''afghanica'' not distinguished.
*''P. n.''  var. ''afghanica'' Aitch. & Hemsl. (syn. ''P. n.'' var. ''thevestina'' (Dode) Bean). Southwest Asia; treated as a [[cultivar]] of ''P. nigra'' by many botanists,<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | ''Populus nigra'' var. ''thevestina'' | 29405 | access-date = December 12, 2017}}</ref> and as a distinct species ''P. afghanica'' by others;<ref name=fp>Flora of Pakistan: [http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=5&taxon_id=200005640 ''Populus afghanica'']</ref> bark smooth, nearly white; leaves and shoots as subsp. ''caudina'' (see also cultivars, below).

The subspecies ''P. n. betulifolia'' is one of the rarest trees in [[Great Britain]] and [[Ireland]],<ref>Milne-Redhead, E. (1990). The B.S.B.I. Black Poplar survey, 1973-88. ''Watsonia'' 18: 1-5. Available [http://www.watsonia.org.uk/Wats18p1.pdf online] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927221812/http://www.watsonia.org.uk/Wats18p1.pdf |date=2007-09-27 }} (pdf file).</ref><ref>Arkive: [http://www.arkive.org/species/ARK/plants_and_algae/Populus_nigra/ ''Populus nigra''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060211162704/http://www.arkive.org/species/ARK/plants_and_algae/Populus_nigra/ |date=2006-02-11 }}</ref> with only about 7,000 trees known, of which only about 600 have been confirmed as female.<ref>Cooper, Fiona (2006).  ''The Black Poplar: Ecology, History and Conservation''. Windgather Press {{ISBN|1-905119-05-4}}</ref>

===Cultivars===
Several [[cultivar]]s have also been selected, these being propagated readily by cuttings:
*'Italica' was originally selected in [[Lombardy]], northern [[Italy]], in the 17th century. The growth is fastigiate (having the branches more or less parallel to the main stem), with a very narrow crown. Common in the [[Mediterranean]] region, it is adapted to hot, dry summers and grows poorly in humid conditions, being short-lived due to [[fungus|fungal]] diseases. It is a male clone.<ref name=bean>Bean, W. J. (1980). ''Trees and Shrubs Hardy in the British Isles'' Vol. 3. John Murray {{ISBN|0-7195-2427-X}}</ref> Around 40 to 50 years, this short-lived variety starts shedding branches and is very likely to be blown over in high winds, each successive tree lost exposing neighbouring trees, creating a domino effect.  
[[Image:Populus nigra-bekes.jpg|thumb|A fastigiate black poplar cultivar of the ''Plantierensis'' group, in [[Hungary]]]]
*''Plantierensis'' group clones are derived by crossing 'Italica' with ''P. nigra'' ssp. ''betulifolia'' at the Plantières Nursery near [[Metz]] in France in 1884; they are similar to 'Italica' (and often mistaken for it), but with a slightly broader crown, and better adapted to the cool, humid climate of northwest Europe, where the true Lombardy poplar does not grow well. Both male and female clones are grown. This is the tree most commonly grown in Great Britain and Ireland as Lombardy poplar.<ref name=bean/>
*'Manchester' is a cultivar of ''P. nigra'' subsp. ''betulifolia'' widely planted in northwest England. It is a male clone, and currently seriously threatened by poplar scab disease.<ref>[[Stace, C. A.]] (1971). The Manchester Poplar. ''Watsonia'' 8: 391-393.</ref><ref>Arboricultural Information Exchange: [http://www.aie.org.uk/trunkline/aie_tr_popscab.html Manchester Poplar Disease] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930072028/http://www.aie.org.uk/trunkline/aie_tr_popscab.html |date=2007-09-30 }}</ref>
*'Gigantea' is another fastigiate clone, of unknown origin, with a rather broader, more vigorous crown than 'Italica'. It is a female clone.<ref name=bean/>
*'Afghanica' (syn. 'Thevestina'): most, if not all, specimens are of a single clone, and many botanists therefore treat it as a cultivar rather than a botanical variety. It is fastigiate, similar to 'Italica', but with a striking whitish bark; it also differs from 'Italica' in being a female clone. This is the common fastigiate poplar in southwest Asia and southeast Europe (the [[Balkans]]), where it was introduced during the [[Ottoman Empire]] period.<ref name=bean/>

==Distribution==
Black poplar has a large distribution area throughout Europe and is also found in northern Africa and central and west Asia. The distribution area extends from the Mediterranean in the south to around 64° latitude in the north and from the [[British Isles]] in the west to [[Kazakhstan]] and [[China]] in the east. The distribution area also includes the Caucasus and large parts of the Middle East.<ref name="broeck03">{{citation |last1=Broeck|first1=An Vanden|title=European black poplar - ''Populus nigra'': Technical guidelines for genetic conservation and use|date=2003|page=6 |url=http://www.euforgen.org/fileadmin//templates/euforgen.org/upload/Publications/Technical_guidelines/927_Technical_guidelines_for_genetic_conservation_and_use_for_black_poplar__Populus_nigra_.pdf |publisher=[[European Forest Genetic Resources Programme]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170119052043/http://www.euforgen.org/fileadmin//templates/euforgen.org/upload/Publications/Technical_guidelines/927_Technical_guidelines_for_genetic_conservation_and_use_for_black_poplar__Populus_nigra_.pdf|archive-date=2017-01-19 }}</ref>
